newsitem.title: USA: West Coast ports back to normal after walkouts.
newsitem.headline: West Coast ports back to normal after walkouts.

text.p: Shipping activity was back to normal Wednesday after a one-day dockworkers strike disrupted activity at ports up and down the West Coast, officials said.
"There was an impact, but it wasn't major," said Yvonne Avila, spokeswoman for the port of Long Beach, the largest port in the U.S. "Everythng is back to normal now."
Most ships had completed loading or unloading before the strike began on Monday, cutting down on delays, Avila said.
The dockworkers walked out on Monday as part of an international job action organized by the International Longshoremen Worker's Union (ILWU) in support of Liverpool, U.K., dockworkers fired in 1995.
The work stoppage, which generally lasted one eight-hour shift at most ports, brought operations to a halt and delayed shipments of cargo coming in and out of the region.
Industry officials said that because the strike occurred on Martin Luther King, Jr. Day, a federal holiday, few complaints were received about import delays.

But for the shipowners who had vessels idled in the port for eight hours, costs could run between $3,000 and $4,000 per hour per ship, said Jay Winter, spokesman for the Steamship Association of Southern California.

In the neighboring ports of Long Beach and Los Angeles between 10 and 15 ships were trapped during the walkout, Winter said. An equal number were probably idled at ports up and down the coast, he said.

A spokesman for American President Lines, one of the largest carriers on the West Coast with operations at Oakland, Los Angeles and Seattle, said it had two ships blocked at the port of Los Angeles as a result of the strike.
The company will try to make up the lost time during transit, the spokesman said.
Meanwhile, union officials said they had no further work stoppages planned for the time being.

"We will continue to help in whatever ways we can with the Liverpool struggle, but at this point there aren't any plans for any more strikes," said Steve Stallone, spokesman for ILWU in San Francisco.
((-- W Pollack, New York Commodities Desk +1 212 859 1640))
